skyline.text: A friend’s thought: today’s chil­dren will never know being lost
Maps India won’t sell sit in a London mu­seum
Borges’s para­ble, and the map that keeps re­draw­ing it­self

masthead.footnote: *It is given for free to users as of today. Page 2

brief.head: Surplus on the map
brief.text: Free Google Maps, Ajay Shah said, gen­er­ates a phe­nom­e­nal con­sumer sur­plus. He once blogged ask­ing whether India’s GDP went up by 0.1 per cent when nav­i­ga­tion ar­rived. {#gdp}

brief.head: No map does it all
brief.text: Google Maps won’t show a dis­trict bound­ary, Ajay Shah said, so if your unit is the dis­trict, it is the wrong map. Every map is a model of the world. {044-C04}

brief.head: The anti-Google club
brief.text: When Apple locked iPod music into its own for­mat, Ajay Shah said, ri­vals ral­lied round MP3. Now Microsoft and Amazon back OpenStreetMap against Google. {044-C10}

brief.head: Spin round Nanda Devi
brief.text: Install the desk­top ver­sion of Google Earth, Ajay Shah urged, on a big screen in ter­rain mode. Rotate around Nanda Devi, “vi­su­al­iz­ing where the plu­to­nium might be hid­ing”. {044-J06}

brief.head: Emperor of everything
brief.text: Shah Jahan, Ajay Shah re­called, was more or less con­vinced that he ruled most of the world. “That’s the main char­ac­ter syn­drome in a ge­o­graph­i­cal sense,” said Amit Varma. {044-J02}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: The way that a map is made, that’s the way a per­son is made.
thought.who: Amit Varma, finding a lesson for life in the patient work of surveyors

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on how India got its maps
lead.head: From Everest to everywhere

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 44

body: Picture your­self as Akbar or Aurangzeb, Ajay Shah said: an em­peror who doesn’t know much about the coun­try he rules. How do you get from A to B? Where do you ford a river, wage a war or build a road?
“There are just thou­sands of ques­tions,” Shah said, “and frankly, you’re just in the dark.”

Maps, he ar­gued, take you from that dark­ness to the light. That was the thread of an hour in which Amit Varma drew out one of Shah’s great loves, from a British sur­vey of 1767 to the phone in your pocket.
## From Clive to Everest
Map-making came to India with the British, Shah said, when Robert Clive com­mis­sioned it in 1767. George Everest later sur­veyed the whole coun­try, and the Survey of India came out of that work.
A map, Shah in­sisted, is not a paint­ing but data. “It’s a list of co­or­di­nates which have cer­tain prop­er­ties.” {044-C02}

Surveying is costly, but once it is done, each extra copy costs al­most noth­ing. That makes maps a pub­lic good, and Shah was blunt about whom it serves: “We don’t give a damn about what the state has in their pocket.” {044-C03}

Free India, he said, let the work slide. In many re­gions, he be­lieves, the last sur­vey dates from around 1934. The sheets were coarse, and maps near the bor­der and the coast could not be sold at all, for fear of ter­ror­ists.

He does not sin­gle out one agency. Monetary pol­icy, the po­lice, the ju­di­ciary, the mil­i­tary and the sta­tis­ti­cal sys­tem all work badly, he said: it is “a part of this un­der­de­vel­op­ment”.
## Maps from orbit

Then tech­nol­ogy changed ev­ery­thing. GPS, satel­lite pho­to­graphs, syn­thetic aper­ture radar, el­e­va­tion maps and the traces of mil­lions of Android phones did away with the need to walk the land with a theodo­lite. {044-C06}
On these, Shah said, three sys­tems have been built: Google Maps, Google Earth and OpenStreetMap. “The peo­ple of India are now in a map par­adise the likes of which we have never seen be­fore.”
It is, he said, an end run around India’s whole prob­lem of state ca­pac­ity, built on pub­lic goods paid for by tax­pay­ers in rich coun­tries. {044-C07}
Varma, read­ing Jorge Luis Borges’s para­ble of a map as big as its em­pire, added that Google Maps es­capes the trap of the static map by up­dat­ing it­self as the world moves.
## Despair, and hope
For Varma, the les­son reached be­yond maps. He said he is full of de­spair about the state of the world, and that tech­nol­ogy is the one thing that gives him hope. {044-C12}

Shah added a cau­tion. The Indian state’s first in­stinct, he said, has been to ban citizens’ map-making, with ter­ror­ism as the ex­cuse for al­most any­thing. Technology needs a lib­eral push­back against the co­er­cive state to go with it.
Varma went fur­ther: the lines on a map are man-made, and his­tory shows they do not last.
Then Varma set his co-host a map quiz. “An exam. An exam. I love exams,” Shah said. “Even if I get zero on five.”
He recog­nised Middle-earth at once, mis­took George Orwell’s *1984* for a map of malaria and guessed fer­til­ity rate for lin­guis­tic di­ver­sity, on which India leads the world.
The last map, of the heights of 19-year-old men, put India near the bot­tom. That, the hosts agreed, is about nu­tri­tion and ill­ness, not genes.

second.label: Property rights
second.head: Toilets by satellite
second.deck: Old Google Earth images won tribals their land, and changed their incentives

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the tribals’ satellite evidence

body: Barun Mitra and his fel­low ac­tivists were fight­ing for tribal land rights, in Gujarat as Amit Varma re­mem­bers it. Varma called it one of the most in­spir­ing sto­ries he had heard, told in the doc­u­men­tary *India Awakes*. {044-R06}

The trib­als had no proof that they had oc­cu­pied the land long enough to qual­ify. So the ac­tivists went back in time with his­tor­i­cal Google Earth satel­lite im­ages, used them as ev­i­dence in court, and won. Ajay Shah added that the team walked the ground with Garmin hand­held GPS units.
In all their years on the land, the trib­als had built few pakka struc­tures and no toi­lets in their homes. Once the right was theirs, they built toi­lets. {044-S03}

quote.text: But the mo­ment they had the land right, the in­cen­tive changed, and they built toi­lets.

third.head: Shorter, without shrinking

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on going from tall to short

body: At col­lege, Ajay Shah was tall for his gen­er­a­tion. Today he is short be­side 20- and 25-year-olds. His height has not changed; the peo­ple around him have grown taller. {044-S08}
“That’s the eco­nomic de­vel­op­ment and the im­prove­ments of India within my life,” he said, “that I’ve gone from being a rea­son­ably tall per­son to being a rea­son­ably short per­son.”

It came up in Amit Varma’s map quiz, whose last map showed the heights of 19-year-old men. Height owes al­most noth­ing to ge­net­ics, Shah said: peo­ple of Indian de­scent raised in ad­vanced economies reach the same av­er­age height. {044-C14} Each child­hood ill­ness in­ter­rupts the use of growth hor­mone.
Varma had seen it him­self. On Bombay’s local trains in the mid-1990s, he no­ticed that peo­ple in first class were taller than peo­ple in sec­ond. Anecdotal, he ad­mit­ted, but stark. {044-S09}

p2.title: Darkness to light
p2.deck: How India went from Akbar’s guesswork to a map paradise, by way of George Everest and Google. {#paradise}

quote.text: So you don’t need to be a local, it is a way of bang­ing away at the na­tivism that oth­er­wise every re­gion suf­fers from.

photo.caption: George Everest, from a photograph taken before 1866

box.title: The man behind the map
box.text: George Everest led the sur­vey that first mapped India, and chose a house in Mussoorie over­look­ing a forested val­ley. Ajay Shah’s pick, John Keay’s *The Great Arc*, tells the story of the early Survey of India: “a heroic tale”. {#greatarc}

sections.label: Before maps
sections.head: Water for horses, or a ford?
sections.caption: the emperor in the dark
body: In the Middle Ages, Ajay Shah said, even an em­peror ruled in the dark. Akbar and Aurangzeb had no way to plan a route, judge a country’s rev­enue or de­cide where a set­tle­ment might go.

What they had was local knowl­edge, held in local lan­guages and gar­bled in trans­la­tion like Chinese whis­pers. “There will be all kinds of con­fu­sion when Tulu is trans­lated into Persian,” he said. One man asks where to water his horses; the other hears, where can the horses ford the river? {044-J01}

Natives might with­hold what they knew, want a rent for it or de­lib­er­ately mis­lead the trav­eller. With only local in­for­ma­tion, Shah said, you are al­ways solv­ing local prob­lems, never see­ing the bird’s-eye pic­ture.
## Boom, you know the an­swer
Maps “abruptly take you from dark­ness to the light”, Shah said. You bum­ble around ask­ing peo­ple, then you look at a map “and boom, you know the an­swer”.

Precision is the point. On a 1:10,000 hik­ing sheet, each cen­time­tre is 100 me­tres; with a com­pass, the map be­comes your guide. A good map, Shah said, means you don’t need a local tracker at all. {#tracker}
~ Amit Varma an­swered with lines from the Magnetic Fields song *The Book of Love*. {044-R02} Love, Shah replied, is as much a mys­tery as ever; our un­der­stand­ing of space has been trans­formed.

quote.text: So you don’t need to be a local, it is a way of bang­ing away at the na­tivism that oth­er­wise every re­gion suf­fers from.

sections.label: The British survey
sections.head: A triangle at a time
sections.caption: the first maps of India
body: Maps came to India with the British, Ajay Shah said, as early as 1767, “a scant ten years after the Battle of Plassey”. Robert Clive com­mis­sioned the work in the parts of Bengal and Bihar they con­trolled. {044-J16}

The great ex­plo­sion came with George Everest. His teams cov­ered the coun­try in in­ter­lock­ing tri­an­gles, about 30 km a side as Shah re­called, and found along the way that the peak now called Mount Everest was India’s high­est point.
## Data, not paint­ings
A printed map, Shah said, is only a paint­ing made out of data: a list of co­or­di­nates with prop­er­ties at­tached. {044-C02}

Surveying a coun­try is enor­mously costly; once it is done, each extra copy costs next to noth­ing. That makes maps a clas­sic pub­lic good, Shah said, and such a good is worth noth­ing if the state keeps it to it­self. {044-C03}

Amit Varma drew a human les­son. The sur­veyor not­ing the height of hills never saw the big pic­ture; he prob­a­bly never saw the fin­ished map. Varma quoted the nov­el­ist E.L. Doctorow: “If you can see the light from your head­lights, you can make the whole dis­tance that way.” {044-J18}
~ Shah drew the same moral from decades of pa­tient sur­vey work: keep build­ing and don’t ask for grat­i­fi­ca­tion. “Don’t look at the num­ber of likes on your Instagram post.” {044-C05}

quote.text: A pub­lic good is for the peo­ple. It’s not there for the state.

sections.label: From the sky
sections.head: Orbiters that only shout
sections.caption: the end of the theodolite
body: A friend once told Amit Varma that peo­ple born today will never know what it is to be lost. Varma called it a mind-blowing thought. {044-S05}

Ajay Shah ex­plained how it hap­pened. The old way needed British lev­els of state ca­pa­bil­ity: thou­sands of peo­ple walk­ing the coun­try with theodo­lites, “ac­cu­rately jot­ting down co­or­di­nates”. Four tech­nolo­gies changed that.

The first is GPS. The US Department of Defense keeps 44 satel­lites aloft, Shah said, and they never talk to your phone. The hand­set hears a few of them and works out its own po­si­tion, to about 10 me­tres. {044-C06}
## Tracing paper in orbit

The sec­ond is satel­lite im­agery. Shah likened it to the translu­cent paper chil­dren lay over a pic­ture: trace the roads and build­ings on a satel­lite pho­to­graph, and you have a first draft of a map.

The third is syn­thetic aper­ture radar, which shows every build­ing in 3D; Shah wants to de­vote a whole episode to it one day. {#sar} The fourth is the dig­i­tal el­e­va­tion map, which es­ti­mates the height of every place.
Add the GPS traces of Android phones, Shah said, and it all adds up to a tech­no­log­i­cal rev­o­lu­tion.
~ GPS alone, Shah said, is more ac­cu­rate than most theodo­lite trigonom­e­try a human map-maker could man­age, though its es­ti­mate of el­e­va­tion is less pre­cise.

quote.text: All they do is shout. They only broad­cast. That’s all. And they don’t know the ex­is­tence of a hand­set.

sections.label: Map paradise
sections.head: Free, as of today
sections.caption: Google Maps, Google Earth and OSM
body: Reforming the Survey of India, Ajay Shah said, would take a gen­er­a­tion of vi­sion­ary lead­ers. Instead, three sys­tems have given Indians bet­ter maps than George Everest ever had.
The first is Google Maps, “a madly great map”, free to users, Shah noted, “as of today”.
Amit Varma brought in Jorge Luis Borges’s *On Exactitude in Science*, the para­ble of car­tog­ra­phers whose map of the em­pire was the size of the em­pire. {044-R05}
Such a map would be out of date the next mo­ment, Varma said. Google Maps gets round that by up­dat­ing it­self, rerout­ing him on the way from Andheri to Bandra East as traf­fic changes. {044-C08}
## Delight on a desk­top

“It is de­light. It is par­adise,” Shah said of the desk­top ver­sion of Google Earth, the sec­ond sys­tem. The third is OpenStreetMap, which Shah called the true dig­i­tal pub­lic good, built by vol­un­teers with no co­er­cion and no tax­a­tion. {044-C09}
None of it used Indian tax money or Indian state ca­pac­ity. “It’s like an end run around the en­tire state ca­pac­ity prob­lem of get­ting the Survey of India to work,” Shah said. {044-C07}
~ Varma pitched a film about two OSM vol­un­teers who meet at a map­ping meetup and go map-making to­gether. Things go wrong, but it ends well: the film is called *Awesome*. {044-J07}

quote.text: It is non-rival, it is non-excludable, it is the dig­i­tal pub­lic good.

sections.label: The one hope
sections.head: Lines that won’t last
sections.caption: technology and the coercive state
body: Amit Varma drew a cau­tion­ary tale from the story. Too many of us take the world as fixed, he said: we as­sume the state must make the maps, and that the state is mori­bund.
He is full of de­spair about the state of the world, he said, but tech­nol­ogy gives him hope. {044-C12} Even the smart­phone, for all its sur­veil­lance and dis­trac­tion, gives peo­ple free­dom.

Ajay Shah put it an­other way: “Our equip­ment is bet­ter than Satyajit Ray. It is our imag­i­na­tions that are the con­straint.” Varma granted the equip­ment, but added that no one is bet­ter than Satyajit Ray. {044-J09}
## The ban re­flex

Then Shah’s own cau­tion. Faced with cit­i­zens mak­ing their own maps, the Indian state’s first in­stinct has been to ban it: pri­vate map­ping, Google Street View, for­eign satel­lite im­agery. “You can ban any­thing under the ex­cuse of ter­ror­ism,” he said. {044-C11}
Technology alone is not enough, he ar­gued: it needs “a large dose of lib­eral phi­los­o­phy”.
Varma won­dered whether, after the crum­bling of the main­stream in media and en­ter­tain­ment, na­tion states might be next. The lines on a map, he said, are man-made and tem­po­rary. {044-C13}
~ Shah has walked to the edge of the India-China bor­der in Ladakh and in Uttarakhand. “It’s just Himalaya,” he said. “There is no line on the map.”

quote.text: All of those lines are tem­po­rary. They are man made and they’re tem­po­rary, that’s what we’ve seen through his­tory. Nothing is per­ma­nent.

Because I think tech­nol­ogy can build the sort of lib­eral world we be­lieve in, and I mean in the clas­si­cal lib­eral sense, tech­nol­ogy can em­power in­di­vid­u­als in a way that po­lit­i­cal move­ments have failed to do.

p3.title: Tales from the map room
p3.deck: Kept, banned, traced and pasted on a wall: four stories of maps

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on his favourite ruin, and what became of it
stories.head: A bungalow before the makeover
body: When George Everest had to choose a place to live, Ajay Shah said, he would have cho­sen the most amaz­ing spot. He picked one in Mussoorie, over­look­ing a val­ley where, Shah seems to re­mem­ber, tigers roamed in those days.
This was the man whose teams had built the first map of the coun­try, and whose name went to India’s high­est point. The house came to be called Everest House.
Many years later it was a run-down old white mar­ble house, tan­gled in legal dis­putes and in a state of decay and dis­re­pair. Yet it was open to the whole pub­lic: any­body could just go there.

Shah loved it. He would sit there, think­ing and dream­ing. “You could feel what it was like to be George Everest,” he said, “to have built the first map of this coun­try, and then to be liv­ing in that bun­ga­low on the edge of that val­ley and the for­est.” {044-S01}
“It was just ab­so­lutely at­mo­spheric,” he said. “My mind would just go wild with the feel­ing of that place.”

He tells it in the past tense, and the rea­son is a sad one. On his last visit, some gov­ern­ment agen­cies were doing ugly and taste­less con­struc­tion to turn the house into a mu­seum. “Unfortunately, it was just ugly.”
~ “These things should re­ally be done by peo­ple who have taste,” Shah said. {#taste} Those who saw the house be­fore, he added, may re­mem­ber it as it was.
stories.why: Some places carry his­tory best when left alone. Restoring her­itage takes taste as well as money, and an of­fi­cial makeover can de­stroy the very at­mos­phere that made a place worth vis­it­ing.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Everest House in Mussoorie

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Survey of India’s forbidden sheets
stories.head: Wanted in Bombay, kept in London
body: When Ajay Shah came to the age of yearn­ing for maps, he dis­cov­ered some very ir­ri­tat­ing things. Many Survey of India sheets were out­dated; in many re­gions, he be­lieves, the last sur­vey was from 1934 or so. {#lastsurvey}
Nor was the scale right. A walker wants 1:10,000 or 1:20,000; the Survey sold 1:200,000, where a cen­time­tre is two kilo­me­tres. Those sheets were “nice, but just un­sat­is­fy­ing”.

Then, “to add in­sult to in­jury”, maps within some 100 km of the bor­der, coast­line in­cluded, could not be sold, lest ter­ror­ists use them. Living in Bombay, Shah was cut off from the coast; hik­ing in the Himalayas, from the bor­der. {044-S02}
~ Yet every Survey of India map, he said, is in a mu­seum in London. “So any self-respecting ter­ror­ist will go to London and get those maps.” {044-J03}
stories.why: A se­cu­rity rule can take a pub­lic good from the cit­i­zens who paid for it while barely slow­ing a real ad­ver­sary. As Ajay Shah put it, “what you end up doing is shoot­ing your­self in the foot”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the maps India wouldn’t sell

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how the world’s map came to be drawn in India
stories.head: Made in Hyderabad, for the world
body: Google started out think­ing, Ajay Shah said, that where a gov­ern­ment re­leased map data, as in the United States and the UK, its work was done.

That ap­proach didn’t scale to coun­tries like India, where the gov­ern­ment ei­ther doesn’t have the data or won’t re­lease it. Sanjay Jain, a pi­o­neer at Google, pushed the com­pany to up its game. {044-S06}

Jain and oth­ers wrote soft­ware, called MapMaker as Shah re­calls. A large fa­cil­ity went up in Hyderabad, where some 5,000 to 10,000 peo­ple, he be­lieves, trace roads, bridges, build­ings and rivers from satel­lite pho­to­graphs.
~ Then come the traces from Android phones. If a phone moves at 60 kph, Shah said, “that’s a mo­torable road”. {#motorable} Shah urged lis­ten­ers to switch off lo­ca­tion track­ing all the same.

quote.text: So they upped their game say­ing, No, we will make the map for the whole world.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Google’s map room in Hyderabad

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the map that started a lifelong love
stories.head: Four sheets, one country, one boy
body: In Ajay Shah’s child­hood home there was a map twice his height. His fa­ther had pasted the four Survey of India sheets that made up the coun­try onto a wooden board and fixed it to the wall.

The boy could not stop look­ing. “I just con­stantly would look at that and try to get a sense of the land and un­der­stand each river,” Shah said. He tried to mug up every dis­trict and place name, and worked out the best routes. {044-S04}
“It was a treat.” Ever since, he has looked for a good mod­ern wall-sized map of India, of National Geographic or Rand McNally qual­ity, and not found one.
~ So he ap­pealed to his au­di­ence: gen­tle reader, if you know of one, tell him. {#wallmap}
stories.why: A small act by a par­ent can start a life­long pas­sion. And even now, some­thing as sim­ple as a good wall map of India is hard to find: Shah has looked ever since, and found none.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his father’s wall-sized map

quiz.q: Who commissioned Britain’s first map-making in India, and how soon after Plassey?
quiz.a: Robert Clive, in 1767, a scant ten years after the bat­tle.

quiz.q: Why could Ajay Shah not buy Survey of India maps of Bombay’s coast?
quiz.a: Maps within about 100 km of the bor­der or coast were banned, cit­ing ter­ror­ists.

quiz.q: Where, by Shah’s account, does Google trace its map of the whole world?
quiz.a: In a large fa­cil­ity in Hyderabad, with per­haps 5,000 to 10,000 peo­ple.

quiz.q: What evidence won tribal land rights in the case Amit Varma described?
quiz.a: Historical Google Earth satel­lite im­ages, which let the ac­tivists go back in time.

quiz.q: In the Borges parable Varma read out, how big was the empire’s map?
quiz.a: As big as the em­pire it­self, co­in­cid­ing with it point for point.

quiz.q: In Varma’s map quiz, what did Shah mistake George Orwell’s *1984* map for?
quiz.a: A map of malaria or yel­low fever, be­fore Varma re­vealed Oceania and Eurasia.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 44. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jorge Luis Borges (Grete Stern, public domain); George Everest (Maull & Polyblank, public domain); Akbar (1605 artist, public domain); Robert Clive (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Satyajit Ray (Dinu Alam Newyork, CC BY-SA 4.0); Robert Bly (Nic McPhee, CC BY-SA 2.0).

shelf.why: It tells the story of the early Survey of India and the first map­ping of the coun­try.

shelf.title: Thelma and Louise
shelf.creator: Ridley Scott
shelf.why: It is one of his favourite films of all time.

shelf.title: On Exactitude in Science
shelf.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
shelf.why: Borges’s one-paragraph para­ble of car­tog­ra­phers whose per­fectly ac­cu­rate map is as large as the em­pire and out of date the next mo­ment: no rep­re­sen­ta­tion can fully cap­ture re­al­ity.

shelf.title: India Awakes
shelf.creator: Free To Choose Network (presented by Johan Norberg)
shelf.why: Johan Norberg’s film tells Barun Mitra’s story of using satel­lite im­agery as court ev­i­dence to win land rights for trib­als, an in­spir­ing case of prop­erty rights chang­ing in­cen­tives on the ground.

shelf.title: Google Maps
shelf.creator: Google
shelf.why: He calls it ‘a madly great map.’ It is free to users and routes you on foot, by car or by pub­lic trans­port through any city.

shelf.title: Google Earth (desktop version)
shelf.creator: Google
shelf.why: Ajay’s ‘paradise’ on a big screen: ter­rain mode, 3D views and aerial fly­bys, plus a prac­ti­cal use for hik­ers, check­ing the el­e­va­tions of sum­mit, base and camp­site be­fore you go.

shelf.title: OpenStreetMap (OSM)
shelf.why: It is the true dig­i­tal pub­lic good: pub­lic do­main, free to down­load, non-rival and non-excludable, and any­one can con­trib­ute.

shelf.title: Did the Indian GDP just jump up by a basis point?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It makes the case that free nav­i­ga­tion cre­ates a huge con­sumer sur­plus for every user, large enough to ask whether it showed up in GDP.

laughs.text: Amit’s pun: ‘And since we all stand on the shoul­ders of gi­ants, it could well be said that Indian map mak­ers since Everest have climbed Mount Everest.’
Amit: ‘if Uber was using Survey of India data, if they had ac­cess to it, you know, you and I would be trav­el­ing by train. So you know thank God for that.’

Following up last week’s ‘sto­ries that should be films’ episode, Amit pitches a new film: two OSM vol­un­teers meet at a map­ping meetup and go map-making to­gether. Things go wrong, but they come back to­gether in the end, be­cause what is the movie called? ‘It’s called Awesome. I just told you.’
Amit on the pos­si­bly apoc­ryphal Saudi cen­sor­ship of a road movie with every shot of women driv­ing re­moved: ‘there­fore Thelma and Louise in Saudi Arabia was four min­utes.’

Amit’s map quiz: Ajay recog­nises Tolkien’s Middle-earth at once (‘the land of Mordor where the shad­ows lie’). He mis­takes George Orwell’s 1984 map of Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia for a map of malaria or yel­low fever. He guesses fer­til­ity rate for a map of lin­guis­tic di­ver­sity, on which India leads the world, even after Amit gives the clue by speak­ing three lan­guages. The last two maps show how moth­ers are treated (India does badly) and the heights of 19-year-old men.
Novelist E.L. Doctorow’s line, quoted by Amit as ad­vice for writ­ers: ‘If you can see the light from your head­lights, you can make the whole dis­tance that way.’
